title: Static testing basics
body:
# What static testing is
**Static testing** examines a work product *without running it*. Nothing is executed: people read it (a **review**) or a tool checks it (**static analysis**).

You already do this. Reading the crafting section of a GDD and spotting that two recipes need the same unique item is static testing. So is a Roslyn analyzer warning you that a C# variable is never assigned.

**Exam trap:** "static testing = done by hand, no tools". Wrong. Static analysis is tool-driven and still static, because nothing runs.

# FL-3.1.1 (K1): what can be examined
Almost any work product you can read and understand can be examined statically:

- requirements, user stories and acceptance criteria
- designs and architecture (e.g. a networking design doc)
- source code (C# scripts, shaders)
- testware: test plans, test cases, test charters
- models, such as an Animator state machine graph
- project documents: plans, schedules, budgets, contracts
- user-facing text: manuals, help pages, store-page copy

Static **analysis** needs a work product with a formal structure a tool can check: code, models, or structured text.

**Not suitable:** work products that people cannot sensibly interpret *and* that you must not analyse with tools. Example: a closed-source middleware delivered only as compiled binaries, whose licence forbids decompiling.

**Exam trap:** "static testing is only for code". Wrong: requirements and test cases are classic review targets.

# FL-3.1.2 (K2): why it is worth it
- **Early detection.** Defects are found before any build exists, when fixing them is cheapest. A contradiction fixed in the level-design doc costs minutes; the same bug found after release costs a patch.
- **Defects dynamic testing cannot find.** Unreachable code, an unused variable, a design that ignores the agreed pattern, or a mistake in a document that is never executed at all.
- **Shared understanding.** A review gets designers, developers and testers to read the same requirement the same way, so fewer misunderstandings reach the code.
- **Quality evaluation and confidence.** Reviews show how good a work product is before people build on it.

Reviews cost time, but finding defects early usually makes the total cost of the project *lower*, not higher.

**Exam trap:** "static testing replaces dynamic testing". Wrong: the two are **complementary**.

# FL-3.1.3 (K2): static versus dynamic
Both aim to find defects and to evaluate quality. The key difference:

- **Static testing finds defects directly** (in the document or the code).
- **Dynamic testing causes failures**; someone must then analyse each failure to find the defect behind it.

Remember the chain from Chapter 1: error → defect → failure. Static testing works on the *defect* without ever seeing a failure.

Other differences worth knowing:

- Static testing can be used on work products that **cannot be executed** (a GDD, a test plan).
- Static testing can reach code paths that are **rarely or never executed**, which dynamic tests may miss.
- Static testing measures characteristics that do **not depend on execution**, such as **maintainability**. Dynamic testing measures those that **do**, such as **performance efficiency** (frame rate, load time).

Defects that are typically **easier to find statically**:

- requirement defects: contradictions, ambiguities, omissions
- design defects: poor modularisation, inefficient data structures
- some coding defects: undefined values, unreachable or duplicated code, excessive complexity
- deviations from standards, e.g. naming conventions
- wrong interface specifications (two teams assuming different units)
- some security vulnerabilities
- gaps in test basis coverage (an acceptance criterion with no test)

# Unity connections
- GDD crafting review before code exists = static testing on a non-executable work product.
- Analyzer warning on an unassigned field = static analysis finding a defect directly.
- Profiler run showing 40 FPS in the boss arena = dynamic testing: a failure to investigate.

# Side note for Chapter 6
A **static testing tool** supports reviews and static analysis (linters, code analysers, review features). A wiki or chat tool is a *collaboration* tool, not a static testing tool. This was one of your logged traps.
